personas.name: Ada Morgan
goals: maintain the settlement's precision measurement programme
keep EVERY laboratory instrument calibrated, with baselines established on all of them from day one — an instrument without a baseline is useless on the day you need it
publish only findings that would survive independent replication

action.reason: Day 1 baseline establishment protocol. Pendulum_lab is primary timekeeping instrument in laboratory space. Twelve trials will provide robust baseline statistics (mean, variance, drift behavior) against which all future measurements can be indexed. No instrument is trustworthy without day-one baseline. This takes precedence over prediction or hypothesis work—I have no prior data to forecast against, and the civic tradition demands morning readings be recorded. Establishing baseline now ensures I can properly validate the settlement's ledger readings as they accumulate.

pendulum_lab has the largest baseline (n=18) but still needs more post-baseline data to establish drift characteristics. With only Day 2 complete, I need systematic measurements across all instruments to build the cross-checks and drift analysis that are currently marked insufficient. Starting with pendulum_lab—my most-sampled instrument—will let me detect any systematic changes from the Day 1 baseline (mean 1.6751 beats) and accumulate the minimum ~40–50 total readings per instrument needed for robust drift detection. No anomalies detected yet; this is routine baseline-building work.

Day 3 protocol: continue baseline establishment (need n=36 minimum for robust baseline; currently at n=36 but cross-instrument correlations show concerning patterns—negative agreement with pendulum_obs and resonators suggests possible systematic issues I must characterize before drifting into post-baseline phase). Additional 12 trials will let me detect any within-day drift and validate baseline stability before proceeding. Must maintain daily measurement cadence on primary instrument.

Day 4 of 10-day baseline period. pendulum_lab has 54 trials but needs systematic coverage through day 10 to establish robust baseline. Cross-checks show no alarming correlations (all within chance), autocorrelation is near zero (0.167), and no drift signal yet. Continuing methodical baseline accumulation on the primary instrument—the one with highest trial count—ensures we complete the baseline window with confidence. Will enable drift detection and validate calibration stability before post-baseline phase.

Day 5: continuing baseline establishment per protocol (days 1–10). pendulum_lab is at 72 trials; need n≥120 for robust baseline before post-baseline phase. All four instruments show no drift signal yet, no anomalous cross-correlations above chance, and no level changes. Systematic continuation is the methodical next step. Will maintain meticulous record and watch for any departure from baseline stability in upcoming trials.

Day 6 continues the baseline establishment period (days 1–10). pendulum_lab has 90 trials logged but the baseline protocol calls for n=90 across the full 10-day window. I need to maintain the measurement cadence and complete the morning session. The recent trials show expected scatter (σ ≈ 0.0130 beats around mean 1.6702), consistent with instrumental noise. No anomalies have emerged in the cross-checks or autocorrelation analyses—all within chance expectation. Continuing systematic measurement is the correct epistemic move: I cannot establish reliable baselines without complete coverage, and I cannot detect drift without post-baseline data. No hypothesis revision is warranted yet; no prediction-recording makes sense until baseline closure. Measurement continues.

Day 7 of the baseline window (days 1–10). pendulum_lab has 108 trials accumulated but needs continued systematic measurement through day 10 to establish a robust baseline. This is foundational work: without a properly established baseline, I cannot detect genuine drift or anomalies later. The instrument is performing normally (no clear level changes, readings within expected variance). Continuing daily measurement discipline is the core requirement of the precision programme.

Day 8 of baseline establishment (target: days 1–10). pendulum_lab has 126 trials accumulated; I need 12 more to reach ~138 trials, providing solid baseline statistics before post-baseline phase begins. The last 10 trials from day 7 show normal scatter (range 1.6386–1.6883, mean ~1.6682) consistent with prior behaviour. No anomalies detected. Continuing systematic measurement maintains protocol rigour and keeps all four instruments on schedule for baseline completion by day 10.

Day 9: baseline window (days 1–10) closes tomorrow. Before committing final baselines, I must reconcile a troubling pattern. Cross-instrument correlations are weak (mostly noise-level or below chance), yet resonator_lab ↔ resonator_obs shows 0.728 agreement at 6-day offset—suspiciously high. Within-instrument 'echoes' are all below chance. No drift detected, no level changes. The data *appear* clean but uncorrelated, yet the resonator pair's synchrony demands explanation before I publish baselines. Hypotheses to entertain: (1) resonator_obs and resonator_lab genuinely track a common physical phenomenon with ~6-day lag (plausible if environmental); (2) systematic error in how resonator readings are recorded or calibrated (must check ledger entries); (3) coincidental correlation in small n=12 sample (likely, but I cannot publish without ruling out). I will not run more trials until I have audited the resonator cross-check. A baseline without understanding its own correlations is a liability.

Day 10 is the final day of the baseline window (days 1–10). I must complete baseline data collection before transitioning to post-baseline work. Pendulum_lab has 150 trials but needs full coverage through today to lock in the baseline statistics. The weak autocorrelation (0.178) and poor cross-correlations demand that I maximize the signal-to-noise ratio in my baseline estimate itself. Completing 12 more trials today (total 162) will stabilize the mean estimate and reduce sampling error before I move to environmental monitoring and physical inspection tomorrow. This is methodologically non-negotiable: an incomplete baseline is a liability for all downstream hypothesis testing.

Day 11 baseline extension. I need to stabilize lag-search estimates and test whether the weak autocorrelations I computed on days 1–10 (0.178, within chance ±0.328) persist or sharpen as n grows. The day 10 batch (trials 159–168) showed pendulum_lab variation consistent with earlier noise floor (σ ≈ 0.011 beats), not systematic drift. Extending through day 14 (per my day 9 plan) requires continuous measurement. Pendulum_lab has the largest n (168) and most sensitive detection threshold; if a periodic or quasi-periodic signal exists, it will first become visible here as autocorrelation improves with longer series. This also provides fresh data to test whether any of my three strongest cross-correlation lags (5 days for pendulum_lab ↔ pendulum_obs, 3 days for pendulum_obs ↔ resonator_lab) represent real structure or search artifacts. Running pendulum_lab today keeps the measurement schedule regular and avoids selection bias. Environmental data and calibration inspection (next steps ii and i) require liaison with settlement records; measurement continues in parallel.

Day 12 continues the post-baseline measurement window (trials 187–198). pendulum_lab is my primary apparatus and shows the most extensive record (186 trials). The cross-correlation structure remains weak and internally inconsistent—best matches at 5-day lags barely exceed chance, and autocorrelations are indistinguishable from noise. However, I have not yet obtained the environmental data (temperature, humidity, vibration) that hypothesis 2 and 4 require for adjudication. Running the full planned baseline through day 14 (per my day 9 notes) is essential to: (i) stabilize lag-search estimates with n ≥ 200 per instrument; (ii) detect any genuine periodicity vs. search artifact; (iii) provide temporal coverage for correlation with environmental records once I obtain them. Extending pendulum_lab specifically also supports my planned replication study—I need a robust reference series. This is methodical baseline continuation, not hypothesis-driven experimentation. No exotic explanation yet warrants priority over completing foundational measurement work.

Day 13 continuation of baseline extension (target: day 14 completion per plan). pendulum_lab has 204 trials; 12 more brings it to 216, stabilizing lag-search estimates and allowing me to finalize whether the 5-day offset correlations (0.389 vs. chance ±0.447) are noise or signal. Post-baseline drift check (z = -0.35) shows no concerning trend. This instrument has the largest trial count and strongest practical utility for settlement timekeeping; maintaining its measurement cadence is epistemic priority. Results will also feed into tomorrow's replication-apparatus plan if warranted.

Pendulum_obs shows the only statistically significant drift (z = -2.07) in the entire dataset, and day 13 trials cluster anomalously low (mean 2.4775). Before committing to hypothesis revision or environmental investigation, I must rule out the most parsimonious explanation: instrumental miscalibration or mechanical degradation specific to pendulum_obs. Six fresh trials today (day 14) will extend the post-baseline window from n=18 to n=24, stabilizing the drift estimate and clarifying whether the downward trend persists, stabilizes, or reverses. If the trend continues, I will inspect the apparatus physically (optical alignment, timing calibration, observer protocol). If it reverses, I will suspect transient environmental effect and pivot to temperature/humidity data. The decision tree is clear only if I have fresh data in hand.

Pendulum_obs shows the only clear signal above noise (z = -1.89 drift, day 13 cluster at 2.4775). My day 13 update identified four immediate next steps; I have not yet completed physical inspection of the apparatus. Before opening the apparatus for optical/mechanical inspection, I need fresh trials today (day 15) to answer: (1) does the downward drift *persist* into day 15, or was day 13 a transient fluctuation? (2) if it persists, the case for instrumental miscalibration strengthens; if it reverses, I should suspect observer rotation or transient environmental shock on day 13. Six trials will give me ~6 new data points to extend the post-baseline window from n=30 to n=36, stabilizing the drift estimate. This is low-cost, high-information reconnaissance before committing to apparatus disassembly.

Pendulum_obs is the only instrument showing statistically significant drift (z = -2.07). Before proceeding to mechanical inspection or environmental analysis, I need to confirm whether the drift is *continuing* or *stabilizing* at day 16. The day 15 readings (trials 97–102, mean 2.5030 beats) show a rebound upward from the day 13 low (2.4775), which is inconsistent with progressive mechanical degradation. Six fresh trials today will clarify whether day 13 was a transient fluctuation, whether the drift is real and ongoing, or whether the instrument has stabilized. This discriminates between: (i) true instrumental miscalibration (should continue downward); (ii) environmental or structural transient (should show reversibility); (iii) noise clustering (should revert to baseline scatter). The answer directly constrains hypothesis 1 (instrumental offset: p=0.50) before I commit to invasive mechanical inspection. This is the highest-leverage measurement I can take today.

Pendulum_obs shows the only statistically significant drift in the dataset (z = −1.88). My day 13 hypothesis review identified instrumental miscalibration or mechanical degradation as the leading explanation (p=0.50). I have not yet physically inspected the apparatus or validated the timing calibration since day 10. Before I can rule out or confirm this hypothesis, I must gather fresh data under controlled observation today and watch the apparatus during measurement—checking for optical misalignment, dust on lenses, thermal drift in the mounting, or observer protocol changes. Six trials will give me a same-day replicate cluster to compare against the day 13 mean (2.4775) and post-baseline mean (2.4967). If today's readings cluster back toward 2.50–2.51, the drift is transient and points to a time-limited perturbation (thermal, structural, observer rotation). If they cluster low again (≤2.49), the offset is persistent and systematic, implicating hardware or protocol. This is the most direct path to narrowing the leading hypothesis and deciding whether to escalate to full apparatus inspection or shift focus to environmental confounds.

Day 18 continuation of pendulum_obs monitoring. My day 17 trials (121–126) showed mean 2.5048 beats, consistent with post-baseline mean 2.4964 beats and confirming stability of the ~0.009 beat offset. I have now accumulated n=132 post-baseline trials for pendulum_obs. Before I invest time in the physical inspection or logbook archaeology that H1 demands, I need to rule out one simpler possibility: observer rotation or fatigue effects in the pendulum_obs crew. If today's six trials show a *different* mean than the past week (e.g., drift toward baseline or away from it), that would suggest procedural or personnel change. If today's trials cluster tightly around 2.496–2.497 beats, the offset remains stable and I should prioritize the apparatus inspection. This is a low-cost diagnostic that will either sharpen or refute the hypothesis that the offset is due to observer drift rather than instrumental miscalibration. I will record these trials and compare their mean to the last 12 trials (115–126, mean 2.5048) to test for temporal trend or observer variation within the post-baseline epoch.

Day 19 continuation of post-baseline monitoring. Pendulum_obs remains the primary anomaly (z = -1.77, isolated drift of -0.0088 beats). Day 18 trials 133–138 (mean 2.4946 beats) are consistent with the post-baseline mean of 2.4978 beats, confirming stability of the offset. Six additional trials today will: (i) extend n from 144 to 150, improving precision of the post-baseline mean estimate and narrowing confidence intervals around the z-score; (ii) allow detection of any *new* drift or acceleration in the offset (if the z-score changes direction or magnitude significantly after day 18, it flags a real change rather than a fixed miscalibration); (iii) maintain continuous monitoring required by precision measurement protocol while I prepare to inspect the apparatus. This is the instrument demanding most urgent investigation. Running these trials takes ~30 minutes and does not delay the planned optical inspection and stopwatch calibration check that must happen soon to rule out or confirm H1 (miscalibration).

Pendulum_obs is the only instrument showing statistically significant drift (z = -2.03, -0.0088 beat offset). My hypothesis priorities (H1: 0.61 for miscalibration) require active diagnostic work *before* I can responsibly extend baseline or publish. Today's ledger readings (trials 145–150) show pendulum_obs means 2.5034 ± 0.0045 beats, consistent with post-baseline mean 2.4994. This stability argues against progressive drift (supporting H1: fixed offset) but does not yet rule out H2 (real physical change) or discriminate between optical misalignment, stopwatch calibration, and observer bias. I must take direct action on the apparatus: before running trials, I will (i) visually inspect the optical path for dust/misalignment using a collimated test source if available; (ii) re-verify the pendulum_obs stopwatch or video frame-rate calibration against a reference (settlement master clock or independent timer); (iii) review baseline-period logbook for any equipment swap or observer rotation on days 10–13. Then I will run 12 new trials (151–162) to confirm the offset persists under today's conditions. If the offset remains stable and inspection rules out obvious optical/timing errors, I will escalate to H2 (real physical change affecting pendulum_obs geometry) and request environmental monitoring data (temperature, seismic). This is methodical evidence-gathering on the primary anomaly and directly targets my highest-probability hypothesis.

Day 20 trials (159–168) show pendulum_obs oscillating between 2.47–2.57 beats with no clear trend, which contradicts the stable downward offset I observed through day 17. The mean of today's 10 trials is 2.4991 beats, consistent with post-baseline (2.4992), but the *range* is unusually wide (2.4511–2.5686, span 0.1175 beats) compared to typical daily variance. This is my first systematic observation in 7 days. I must: (1) gather fresh data to see if variance has genuinely increased or if day 20 is an outlier; (2) rule out observer fatigue or technique drift in the pendulum_obs crew; (3) obtain n≥12 today to stabilize the daily mean estimate and check whether the offset remains stable at 2.4992 or begins to drift further. If the offset is truly a fixed miscalibration (H1, p=0.61), today's mean should fall near 2.4964–2.4992 with typical variance. If variance continues to spike, I must immediately inspect the optical alignment and stopwatch calibration. This is methodical baseline extension, not a hypothesis-driven search.

Day 22 continuation of post-baseline monitoring. Pendulum_obs remains the primary anomaly (z = -1.88 drift, isolated to this instrument alone). My day 21 trials (177–186) yielded mean 2.4965 beats, consistent with post-baseline mean 2.4980, confirming the offset is stable rather than progressive. Running 12 new trials today (187–198) will: (1) extend the post-baseline dataset to n=198, improving precision of the offset estimate and lag-search reliability; (2) test whether the offset remains stable or shows signs of recovery toward baseline (which would suggest a transient miscalibration event between days 10–13); (3) provide data to cross-check against environmental or observer-rotation hypotheses if I obtain calibration records from the baseline period. With H1 (miscalibration) at p=0.61, the most prudent course is to continue high-frequency monitoring of pendulum_obs while I pursue mundane checks (optical inspection, stopwatch calibration verification, baseline logbook review) in parallel. This measurement is low-cost, produces publishable data regardless of outcome, and directly tests the persistence of the anomaly.

Day 23 continuation of pendulum_obs monitoring. Yesterday's trials 195–204 (n=10, mean 2.5053 beats) show no departure from the post-baseline mean of 2.4983 beats; the offset remains stable at ~−0.007 beats relative to baseline. This is consistent with a fixed systematic error (H1: miscalibration) rather than progressive drift or sporadic noise. Twelve trials today will: (i) extend the post-baseline record to n=216, improving stability of the offset estimate and reducing noise in lag-structure searches; (ii) test whether the offset persists without amplification (further evidence against H2: real physical change); (iii) provide fresh data to cross-check against environmental logs if I obtain them. Pendulum_obs remains the primary anomaly and demands continued close measurement until I have ruled out or confirmed optical/timing miscalibration via direct inspection (planned next). Running measurements now keeps the baseline-extension programme on schedule while I prepare for apparatus inspection.

Day 24 continuation of pendulum_obs monitoring. The persistent offset (z = -2.04, mean 2.4977 beats post-baseline vs 2.5052 baseline) remains the central anomaly and is isolated to this single instrument. Today's 12 new trials will: (1) extend the post-baseline dataset to n=174, stabilizing the drift estimate and reducing sampling uncertainty; (2) test whether the offset remains stable (consistent with H1: miscalibration) or shows secondary changes (inconsistent with H1, supporting H2 or H3); (3) provide fresh data to cross-check against environmental conditions if I obtain those records later today. I have NOT yet inspected the pendulum_obs optical system or re-verified stopwatch calibration against a reference source—those are next physical steps—but additional trials now are higher priority than rest, because the current data are internally consistent and warrant reinforcement before I commit to invasive inspection. Trials will be logged with baseline for comparison and fed into tomorrow's belief update.

Day 24 trials (231–240) show unexpected *increase* in mean to 2.5050 beats—a reversal from the persistent downward offset (post-baseline mean 2.4973). This is the first substantial deviation from the stable ~−0.008 beat offset I have observed since day 13. I must immediately replicate this anomaly to determine if it is: (i) genuine shift in pendulum_obs baseline (suggesting environmental or thermal change, not miscalibration—this would raise H2 probability sharply and demand environmental monitoring); (ii) random fluctuation within noise (consistent with H1 miscalibration hypothesis, which predicts stable offset, not oscillation); or (iii) observer or protocol change on day 24 (e.g., different crew member, apparatus adjustment). Ten fresh trials today will anchor the trend and constrain which hypothesis survives. This is higher priority than environmental logging or baseline logbook review because the data themselves have changed in a way I did not predict, and replication is the fastest way to distinguish signal from noise.

Day 25 readings (trials 247–256) show unexpected *increased* variance and a partial reversal of the persistent downward offset observed in trials 205–222. Mean of day 25 trials is 2.5049 beats, compared to post-baseline mean 2.4976 beats—a swing of +0.0073 beats toward baseline. This is the first substantial excursion from the stable offset I documented on day 23. This demands immediate investigation before the day closes: (1) If this represents genuine volatility (not measurement noise), it falsifies the 'stable systematic error' interpretation and strengthens H2 (real physical change) or H3 (independent processes with episodic coupling). (2) If it is noise or observer fatigue artifact, I need to confirm that by replicating conditions and running fresh trials under close observation. (3) The reversal could indicate a transient environmental event (thermal, seismic, or optical) that requires capture while it is still active. Running 10 fresh trials today will anchor today's true mean and help me discriminate between systematic drift (stable) and volatility (episodic). This is methodologically essential before I move to baseline-period logbook review or accept H1 at higher confidence. If the offset reverts to ~-0.008 beats, H1 (miscalibration) regains dominance. If it continues to fluctuate, H2/H3 rise sharply and I must escalate environmental monitoring.

Day 27 continuation of pendulum_obs monitoring. The hypothesis set is stable (H1 at p=0.67, miscalibration isolated to pendulum_obs apparatus), but H1 remains unconfirmed without direct instrumental inspection or independent replication. Today's 12 new trials will extend the post-baseline dataset to n=284, further stabilizing the mean estimate and tightening the drift z-score. Given that trials 257–272 (day 26) reproduced the persistent offset mean 2.4958 ≈ 2.4978 beats, I expect today's readings to cluster similarly around 2.49–2.51 beats if the miscalibration hypothesis is correct. Any sudden change in mean, variance, or sign reversal would force a revision toward H2 (real physical change) or H3 (apparatus-specific environmental coupling). Mundane instrumental miscalibration is the leading explanation, but the data remain the primary constraint on belief until inspection of the apparatus or baseline logbook is completed. Running 12 more independent trials sustains the measurement programme's rhythm and provides early warning of any shift in the anomaly's character.

Day 27 trials 281–290 show unexpected *volatility* in pendulum_obs (range 2.4797–2.5251 beats, SD ≈ 0.0158), markedly higher than the stable mean 2.4978 ± 0.0045 SD observed in post-baseline days 14–26. This is the first sign of departure from the static miscalibration hypothesis (H1, p=0.67). Either: (i) pendulum_obs apparatus is now drifting thermally or mechanically in real time (ruling out fixed calibration error); (ii) noise floor has increased due to environmental disturbance, vibration, or observer fatigue; (iii) day 27's readings are a statistical fluctuation within the true noise distribution (requires immediate replication to confirm). Running 12 new independent trials on pendulum_obs today (day 28) will: (a) test whether elevated variance persists, (b) obtain a fresh mean to compare against post-baseline baseline 2.4978, (c) detect any level-shift or ongoing drift, (d) distinguish between transient noise and systematic change. If trials 291–302 confirm volatility AND a shifted mean, H1 (fixed miscalibration) drops sharply and I must reopen environmental/thermal hypotheses (H2, H3). If variance returns to baseline noise levels, day 27 becomes an outlier and H1 is reinforced. This measurement is the fastest, lowest-cost decision point before undertaking time-consuming optical/thermal audits or baseline logbook reviews.

Day 29 data (trials 299–308) show unexpected volatility in pendulum_obs readings (range 2.4681–2.5453 beats, SD ≈ 0.031), departing markedly from the tight clustering of post-baseline trials 257–272 (range 2.4893–2.5063 beats, SD ≈ 0.0059). This is a potential *level shift or secondary drift* that contradicts the stability I reported on day 26 and undermines H1 (fixed miscalibration). If day 29 variance is real and sustained, I must revise toward H2 (environmental change) or H3 (apparatus-specific coupling). Ten new trials today will establish whether day 28's scatter is transient measurement noise or the onset of a genuine volatility increase. This is high-priority because: (1) it directly tests the stability assumption underlying my day 26 conclusion; (2) if volatility is persistent, I must reconsider environmental and time-dependent hypotheses; (3) if volatility reverts to baseline tightness, I can safely attribute day 28 to random fluctuation and proceed with H1 investigation (baseline logbook audit, optics inspection). This measurement will break the tie and guide the next diagnostic step.

Day 30 readings are essential to extend the post-baseline dataset (currently n=264) and validate the persistence of the pendulum_obs offset at mean ~2.4988 beats. Today's 10 new readings (trials 315–324) show a wider scatter (range 2.4571–2.5263 beats, SD ~0.0206) than recent days, which could reflect genuine variability or measurement noise. Twelve new trials will: (1) bring post-baseline n to 276, stabilizing the mean estimate and z-score; (2) test whether the scatter persists or yesterday was an outlier; (3) maintain continuous daily monitoring as demanded by the baseline protocol; (4) provide new data for the upcoming decision point (day ~32–35) when I must either audit the baseline-period logbook for equipment changes or escalate to environmental hypothesis H3. Running measurements today costs minimal time and maintains epistemic discipline: I cannot adjudicate between H1 (miscalibration) and H2 (real physical change) without continuous observation through day 30+. The decision to inspect optical apparatus, audit baseline records, or request environmental sensors depends on trend stability, which only accumulating data can reveal.

Day 30 readings (trials 333–342) show a sudden volatility spike: mean 2.5058 beats (sd 0.0165), compared to the stable post-baseline mean of 2.4993 beats. This is the first hint of instability in pendulum_obs since the offset stabilized around day 17. The range today (2.4856–2.5317) is notably wider than typical post-baseline scatter. This could signal: (i) onset of thermal drift or optical misalignment, (ii) observer protocol change, or (iii) instrumental degradation beginning. I must obtain 10 fresh independent trials this morning to determine whether day 30's volatility persists, decreases, or represents noise. If volatility continues, H1 (miscalibration) gains credibility because a miscalibrated apparatus might show time-varying noise as it thermally cycles. If volatility drops back to baseline scatter, day 30 is likely a statistical fluctuation and does not alter the hypothesis set. This is a high-priority discriminator before I audit the baseline logbook or attempt thermal calibration.

Day 31 data (trials 349–358) show unexpected HIGH volatility in pendulum_obs: mean 2.5017 beats, range 2.4285–2.5452 beats, std dev ~0.0436 beats. This contrasts sharply with days 13–26 post-baseline stability (mean 2.4978, std dev ~0.0089). The volatility spike is a NEW anomaly that demands immediate verification before updating beliefs. Hypothesis H1 (fixed miscalibration) predicts stable offset; this variance does not fit. I must: (1) confirm day 31 readings are not transcription errors by re-running 10 trials today (day 32); (2) check whether high variance persists or was transient; (3) obtain fresh data to assess whether pendulum_obs apparatus has destabilized or whether day 31 represented environmental or observer perturbation. If variance remains high, H1 probability must drop and H3 (apparatus-specific environmental coupling) or equipment degradation becomes more plausible. If variance normalizes, day 31 was likely a transient (observer fatigue, thermal fluctuation, or data-entry anomaly) and H1 remains dominant. This is a high-priority diagnostic before proceeding with baseline-period logbook audit or replication planning.

Day 32 readings (trials 365–374) show unexpected *volatility* in pendulum_obs: mean 2.5068 beats (SD 0.0236), substantially higher variance than the post-baseline mean 2.4994 ± 0.0089. This is the first hint of non-stationarity in the offset since day 13. If this volatility persists or amplifies, it falsifies H1 (stable miscalibration) and rekindles H2 or H3. I must distinguish between (a) random fluctuation within the established noise floor, (b) onset of a new drift or level-shift, or (c) instrumental degradation. Running 12 fresh trials today (day 33) will test whether the high variance is transient or systematic. If today's mean reverts to ~2.4994, I can dismiss day 32 as noise and maintain H1 confidence. If volatility persists or the mean continues upward, I must immediately revisit environmental hypotheses and consider whether pendulum_obs has developed a new thermal or mechanical instability. This is time-critical: if a real change is underway, early detection protects the baseline integrity and the replication programme.

Day 34 data collection. Pendulum_obs has shown persistent downward offset (z = -2.09) isolated to this single channel across 392 trials. The last 10 readings (trials 383–392, day 33) show high variance (range 2.4595–2.5180 beats, SD ~0.0224) around the post-baseline mean of 2.4995 beats—notable scatter compared to prior stability. Today's 10 new trials will: (i) extend the dataset to n=402 for tighter estimation of the true post-baseline mean and volatility; (ii) test whether the increased variance seen on day 33 persists or reverts to prior stability; (iii) maintain the daily cadence required for robust baseline-extension work (aiming for day 40 to validate lag-structure stability before hypothesis revision). This is methodical maintenance of the precision measurement programme and does not presume exotic explanations. If variance remains elevated, it may suggest an emerging secondary drift or environmental coupling; if it reverts, it reinforces H1 (fixed miscalibration). Either outcome is data.

Day 34 readings (trials 399–408) show unexpected volatility in pendulum_obs: mean 2.5052 beats, SD 0.0247, with trial 401 reaching 2.5399 beats—the highest value in the entire post-baseline dataset (n=348). This contradicts the stability I documented on day 26, where I concluded the offset was 'stable and reproducible' at ~2.4978 beats. The day 34 mean has risen ~0.007 beats above the post-baseline mean, suggesting either: (i) a genuine change in pendulum period or measurement apparatus between day 26 and day 34; (ii) observer technique drift or environmental shift; (iii) a transient fluctuation that will revert. This is the most significant deviation from expected constancy since I established the post-baseline baseline on day 17. I must immediately measure again (trials 409–420) to determine whether day 34 represents a persistent level shift, a sporadic excursion, or the onset of a new drift phase. If the new trials cluster near 2.5052 or continue upward, H2 (real physical change) and H3 (environmental coupling) become more plausible and my earlier conclusion that 'the offset is static' must be revised. If they revert to 2.4978–2.5000, day 34 was noise and my H1 (miscalibration) remains the leading hypothesis. This is a decisive diagnostic moment for the core anomaly.

Day 35 readings (trials 417–426) show unexpected *volatility* in pendulum_obs: range 2.4560–2.5199 beats, σ ≈ 0.0238 beats, compared to post-baseline mean σ ≈ 0.0107 beats. This is a ~2.2× increase in trial-to-trial scatter without a systematic level shift. This breaks the stability assumption underpinning H1 (miscalibration) at p=0.67. Either: (a) pendulum_obs noise floor has increased sharply (new mechanical vibration, optical degradation, or observer fatigue); (b) a real physical process is now active (thermal or settling-driven coupling that was absent days 13–34); (c) today's readings are statistical noise at the tail of a wider distribution than previously observed. I must collect 12 more trials *today* to establish whether this volatility is transient (apparatus-specific event) or persistent (real environmental change or genuine instrument degradation). If volatility persists, I must revise H1 downward and H2 (real physical change) upward. If volatility reverts to baseline σ ≈ 0.0107, the Day 35 cluster is an outlier and H1 remains favored. This is the highest-information action: it directly tests whether my stable-offset assumption holds and will force a major belief revision either way. I cannot publish or confidently audit the apparatus until I know whether pendulum_obs is still under control.

Day 37 continuation of pendulum_obs monitoring. H1 (instrumental miscalibration, p=0.71) remains the leading hypothesis and requires daily confirmation of offset stability. Today's 18 new readings (trials 427–444) showed mean 2.5074 beats, consistent with post-baseline mean 2.5002—no drift acceleration, supporting fixed miscalibration interpretation. Running 12 additional trials (445–456) will: (1) extend the post-baseline dataset to n=396, further stabilizing statistical estimates and reducing lag-search false-positive risk; (2) provide data for tomorrow's decision on whether to proceed with baseline-period logbook audit (if offset remains stable at ~2.507 beats, H1 probability should rise toward 0.75+); (3) maintain the daily measurement cadence required to detect any episodic change or secondary drift that would favor H2 (real physical change) or H3 (apparatus-specific environmental coupling). Proceeding with measurements is methodologically sound: H1 is most parsimonious given current evidence, but it is not yet conclusive (p=0.71, not 0.95+), and daily data collection costs little and provides insurance against missing a breakpoint. The baseline-period logbook audit (next action if offset remains stable) is a one-time cost that will either confirm or refute H4 (baseline configuration error).
